newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Czech c.bank wants consensus to stem wage rises.
newsitem.headline: Czech c.bank wants consensus to stem wage rises.

text.p: The Governor of the Czech National Bank said he is concerned about the rapid growth of wages, but the modest state-sector pay raises in the draft 1997 budget were a relatively positive sign.

In a taped interview with Reuters Financial Television to be broadcast later, Tosovsky said Czech officials should seek a consensus on wage rises between business and labour, but he said he did not support new government wage controls.
"We don't think that some sort of administrative regulation would help, but it's possible we can try some other mechanism to try do reduce the increase in wages," Tosovsky said.
"One possibility is that we should try to reach a consensus with entreprenuers and with trade unions, but the question is whether this is politically acceptable."
Average state sector wages rose, in nominal terms, 24.7 percent in the first half of the year, compared with 17.6 percent in the overall economy.
Until 1995, the Czech government would fine enterprises who could not prove that the average of pay rises were not matched by increases in productivity.

The 1997 draft state budget, which has been approved in the first reading by parliament but still faces two more readings, calls for average nominal state sector pay increases of 12.4 percent, and an expected overall nominal rise of 13.8 percent.

The 1996 pay rises, not matched by an increase in productivity, have accelerated an already large trade deficit, sparked domestic demand which has in turn caused higher inflation and made exported goods less competitive.
"I can see that wages are growing quite fast... but in the budget for next year the growth in (state sector) wages is much more modest than this year," Tosovsky said.
"It's always relative, it's better than the current situation. What I am not sure of is that the private sector will follow the public sector."
